85.q: Yeah, Jimmy Dorsey, Jack Teagarden. Those two stand out in my mind, those two particularly. There were others that I can’t think of by name at the moment.

85.s: Carter says he never thought of mixed-race sessions as unusual.
85.q: I didn’t know anything about that idea of touring. I just did a record session, and that’s all I remember. There may have been some talk otherwise.

527.t: Miles on the white players in Birth of the Cool
527.s: Farmer repeats his question to Miles and the lesson that only the music counts.
527.q: Yeah, I asked Miles, “What are you doing recording with these white cats in the band, like Lee Konitz and Gerry Mulligan?” He said, “I don’t care what color anybody is.” Later on, all this press about he’s got to kill a white man before he dies and all kind of stuff like that, but as far as the…

527.t: Bill Evans at Birdland and Miles's attitude to race
527.s: Evans nearly quit a Birdland gig over a remark about race and Farmer told him to finish; Miles said colour was irrelevant.
527.q: That’s where I met Bill was through George, and then I was doing some off- nights at Birdland. Interesting[ly], I decided one time I would call Bill and get him to make the Monday night with me. He came up to me after the first set and said, “Art, I’m not able to finish the gig. I’m gonna go home.”…

26.t: The band's mix of skin colours and backgrounds
26.s: Duke hired for talent regardless of colour; band included Creoles, Puerto Ricans and West Indians.
26.q: If Duke liked the way you played, he didn't care how you looked. That was it. He didn't care how you looked, he took talent. Duke always -- his god was talent. He could single out a guy who you would say, this cat can't play nothing. But he could see something in him. He was just a genius like…

26.t: Why Ivie Anderson, not May Alix
26.s: Greer repeats the story of choosing Ivie because May Alix looked white.
26.q: That's right. No, no, the only thing Duke kind of drew the line on, that's how we got Ivie, you see, May Alex, the girl I was telling you about, the singer, a very -- she come to New York and was a sensation. But she was a girl, you couldn't tell if she was white or colored.

29.t: Sitting in with white bands at the Cotton Club
29.s: Howard confirms he sat in with white bands as a guest for a tune or two, with no mixed steady jobs then.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Come to (inaudible) place and come back and play again. Like, get back and play something that they wanted to play, that I could play.

386.s: Price opines on Mezz's identification and musicianship, with jokes.

386.t: Benno Kennedy and Price's claim that jazz is a black tradition
386.s: After praising trumpeter Benno Kennedy he rebuts the teacher who said he lacked musicality and argues jazz is rooted in black heritage.

And...I think that playing music, Dan, can become contagious and then, if you have any insight or any...this damn guy…

388.t: Acceptance by black musicians and Leeman's racial outlook
388.s: Leeman says he had no racial problems; black musicians took him under their wing, and Ellington and Basie were his idols.
388.q: MR. LEEMAN: I don't want anybody to get the wrong idea of how I put this together. As I said before, I had no background with racial disturbance, and when I went to Kansas City and made all these beautiful friends and all these wonderful people who took me with open arms and under their wing,…

388.t: Working with so many black musicians: Leeman's view
388.s: Leeman says black musicians liked his playing first, quoting Dan Morgenstern that Condon ignored race as if it did not exist.
388.q: There's been an urgent prodding in the base of my mind or in the back of my mind, I should say, to get this off my chest. The black and white issue, or -- if you wish, the problems involved in my career racially.

413.t: Prejudice in reverse; Hinton's side of eating apart
413.s: Maxwell admits to overcompensating around Black musicians; Hinton explains why he stayed away from dinners for the white players' sake.
413.q: So all my favorites were that. And I'll tell you, it took me many years to get mad at a black guy, to be able to tell him to go screw himself, you know, because I was always sort of backing off. So in other words, I had a prejudice in reverse, there was a difference in my mind. It took me many…

413.t: Black musicians' edge on jazz; culture not inheritance
413.s: Neighbors teased him about liking Black musicians, and he argues the jazz edge is cultural since kids of all colors keep time.
413.q: But there was this thing about it. I know I was kidded in my hometown because my neighbors would say, "Well, you're never going to be happy until you have a green suit and play with a nigger band, or something." And I said, that's right, you know. Or guys would kid me, I'd see a black girl and say…

76.t: Loving the music regardless of the person; Zutty's color-blindness
76.s: Dance and Paul Gonsalves say you may love someone's music whatever his character; Marge says Zutty never saw color and treated white musicians as friends.
76.q: And Zutty has always done that all his life. Color didn't make any difference, to him. He wasn't thinking of that like these militants. He loved the white ones as much as he loved the black boys. If they could play, if they were his friends, they were his friends.

76.t: Getting Mel Powell started at Nick's
76.s: Zutty brought the white pianist Mel Powell to play at Nick's, and Nick objected to a white boy with a Black band, so Zutty let him play one night and told Nick it was him, not the customers.
76.q: And that's the way he's been and he had so many knocks from them same ones that he has upheld. They didn't know it, the love that Zutty had in his heart for them. As I say, he never was an Uncle Tom or anything, but he loved his, he got Mel Powell started.

86.s: Dance and Edison recall bands that preferred light-skinned players, with Sandy Williams' joke about Taft Jordan.
86.q: Yeah, Noble Sissle -- all of them were very light in that band. Alphonso Trent's band, most of them was light, most of them was real light. I think Snub Mosley was the darkest guy in the band.

529.t: White hopes and Miles's band: making room for white stars
529.s: Sam believes writers had to move black bands aside to make room for Mulligan, Chet Baker and Getz, and says Miles's band blocked it.
529.ch: Race, critics and the big bands
529.q: I have to talk about the laymen men because he's the man that takes care of us, you know. So these writers started writing about these freedom players, you see. And yeah, I do believe that it was a conspiracy and that because in order for the white musician to get a play, they had to get all these…

529.t: Why black influence goes unadmitted, Getz and Lester Young
529.s: Sam and Ridley say egos and race keep players like Getz from crediting black influences.

917.t: Big Eye Louis, the Barquets and a clarinetist who crossed over
917.s: Asked about Louis Nelson's father; Keppard recalls a clarinetist who passed into white bands for more money, was found out and left for Chicago and California.
917.ch: New Orleans clarinetists and learning the guitar

One of them used to play a lot of bands, you know, on the other side. Yeah. Of course, I understand he's right between lines…

622.t: White and Black musicians kept apart in Chicago
622.s: Ashcraft says white musicians seldom connected with Black bands like Oliver's, with separate unions and Black bands seen as entertainers.
622.ch: Friars Inn, NORK and Chicago influences
622.q: Yeah. That's why I don't, I think that it wasn't until after Bud, Tesh, and the others had heard Louie, or rather heard the Oliver Band, out in the south side, that they really connected the two up. And I'm not too sure they did. They were inclined to separate the white and Negro musicians, partly…

82.t: Small-band stars and Bill Moore as first Black player in a white band
82.s: The Ramblers' soloists could read-and-play with no rehearsal and publishers used them to okay arrangements. Kirkeby claims Bill Moore was the first Black musician in a big white band, before Goodman.

769.t: Treatment around the world and segregation in Louisiana
769.s: He enjoyed everywhere, was treated well abroad, avoided fishing-island towns after what happened to Papa Celestin's band, and says jazz has helped integration.
769.q: Well, I'm going to tell you the truth, Tom. I enjoyed them all. I really did enjoy them all. I don't think one I did the other. But everywhere we went, we were treated royally. Nobody scorned us because we were what we are. Nobody overlooked us or nothing. They really enjoyed our playing. They…

240.t: Cuckoo Chalmers, white musicians, and crossing the color line
240.s: He recalls neighbor Cuckoo Chalmers, how little Black players knew white musicians, a few names, and people passing across the color line.
240.ch: Bunk Johnson and the New Orleans scene
240.q: Well, I don't really know. Because I never heard him. I started, uh... I don't know about his technique or on. I couldn't say anything about that. He had to play one number in my life, just a lot of that. I never heard. Do you have any records on? Oh, yeah. No. Uh, I know about Cornell and them…

251.t: Reception in New Orleans, prejudice and music
251.s: Albert drew crowds in New Orleans clubs but recalls prejudice there and in San Antonio, and says music and sports have fought it.

However, let me say this, that I have met up with a lot of great response when I had my band, when I came back to New Orleans, even though I was considered a Texas boy, by Texans and other people, but whenever I played here, the Santa Cendez…

37.t: Where the white Chicago hot style came from

763.t: Did only Black musicians play early jazz? Tempo and race
763.s: Asked about white musicians in early jazz, he rejects the idea that Black players kept better tempo and says imitation is no good.
763.q: No, that was really wrong. I never did want to come out with that discussion, because you have so many people that contradict you about that. But when they tell you that a colored man can play a better strict temper than a white man, don't let nobody kid you about that. That really is a bad face…

2.t: Bill Johnson's light skin and passing
2.s: Hogan and Russell discuss Johnson passing for white and compare complexions, including Don Albert.
2.q: Yes, he's never heard of it. He didn't know he was in San Antonio. So Don, of course, is light enough to pass, too. He wouldn't have to be afraid to talk to Don, but he's passing, evidently. But with that age and his memory gone, evidently.

121.t: Creole caste and the Autocrat back door

And now, to show you how much things have changed, the president is a POA number one black dude. In color, I'm talking about he's black. Yeah. He's…

288.s: They talk of the two Moret brothers, one who could pass, and others such as Matoyi and Mario Bradley.

681.t: First playing with a Black musician, with Louis Prima in 1937
681.s: He never played with a Black musician in New Orleans; the first time was with Prima's band in California in 1937.

Oddly enough, when I first, when I went to California with Louis Prima in 1937, we had a piano player, I don't remember his name, but he was a great piano, relief piano player. 635.t: Uniforms outdoors, Lincoln Park and race and color in New Orleans
635.s: Uniforms were for street work and Lincoln Park picnics; talk turns to the mixed audience, light-skinned Creoles, his white wife and his Indian mother, and a doctor's record party.
635.q: Well, we didn't wear the uniform in the club. We wore the uniforms that we played. In the streets. In the streets. We didn't, but, see, when we played in the club, after we come out of the club, we had so much, you see, we had so much work that we wore uniforms. Like, we would most of the players…

290.t: Light-skinned musicians passing in white bands
290.s: Light-skinned Black musicians such as Arnold Metoyer and Eddie Cherrie played in white bands; Achille Baquet.

855.t: Whether only Black musicians play New Orleans music; tone differences
855.s: He believes New Orleans music belongs in New Orleans and hears differences in tone and vibrato between white and Black players.

Aber ich glaube, dass nur schwarze Musiker eben hier nur Leans diese Art von Musik machen können. Auch wenn ich hier die weißen Musiker gehört habe, ist doch ein Unterschied. 54.t: Getting along with the white community in Natchez

I don't know, it seems like that, uh, if I have to say it with you gentlemen, sure, that, uh, I was a pretty quiet fella…

837.s: Russell says some light-skinned musicians passed for white. Souchon recalls Tom Brown's slur against Laine and wonders about others, including Yellow Nunez.

129.t: Racial attitudes: growing up without prejudice and touring with a Black rhythm section

674.t: A hippie on the Ellington bus and the trip to Ethiopia
674.s: Asked about fitting in with older black musicians, he says he was a long-haired hippie, never judged, and recalls Barrie Lee Hall, Cootie Williams and the palace of Haile Selassie.

791.t: Race and covert control in the New York scene

437.t: Race in jazz and young musicians
437.s: He says he sees people as people, and discusses experimentation by younger players that record companies will not release.

437.q: I have a friend who’s a drummer. He happens to be a person of color, and I don’t even like to say that to be honest with you because I look at people as people and I’ve never met a man I don’t like, Will Rogers. It’s however they act and treat me that will judge that in the end. But I’ve been in…

67.t: Paul Whiteman's band and a light-skinned black trumpeter
67.s: Whiteman and Ted Lewis each hired a black trumpet player who could pass for white.

131.t: Charlie Shavers in the Dorsey band and race in the band
131.s: Asked about Charlie Shavers as the one black player in the Dorsey band, he recalls the Marie arrangement and says race meant little to him.

605.t: Encouraging students and the lack of a black-white divide among musicians
605.s: Clark Terry and WDR, musicians of earlier generations ignored race, and stories of Cedar Walton being asked about a white tenor player.

132.t: No colour line among swing fans, and friendship with Joe Williams

420.t: Racism in jazz and the Lewinsky affair

981.t: Pay scales, unions and race in Cincinnati and New York

981.q: Yeah but that was just between Kentucky and — but generally speaking, yes. The white musicians made more. Even their scale, we had two different unions.

559.t: Dizzy's Bahai faith and absence of racial tension in the group

540.t: Does race matter for young jazz musicians today?

91.s: White players sat in in Harlem but black players could not go downtown; musicians resigned themselves to the system.
91.ch: Harlem scene and race in music
91.q: But the opportunity was denied them. In addition to the fact that in Harlem, many white musicians used to come in and listen to the black musicians, and not only listen, but sit in with them. Quite often. But we couldn't go downtown and sit in with them.

418.t: Contact between black and white musicians and integration
418.s: Contact between the races began to improve in the late Twenties; the real change in the music came around 1935-36 with Dizzy and Parker, and integrated bands today work better.
418.ch: Records, dances and Blanche Calloway (repeated passages)
418.q: It wasn't as much as it should have been. It started getting better. In the late Twenties, it started to get a little better.

235.t: Being the only Black man in club-date bands; Bill Dillard
235.s: He was hired because he could entertain as well as play, alongside Bill Dillard, and had earlier played with white musicians like Zoot Sims and Al Cohn.
235.ch: After the Paradise: club dates and Virginia
235.q: Yeah, well that was because I could entertain. You see what I mean? Well, they knew I could play the music...I had to know the music, but I could entertain too. So that was doin' two for one. I was doin' a double.

611.t: Goldkette's band and merging technique with soul
611.s: Of the white dance bands, Jean Goldkette's impressed him most; Waters argues he studied more than most Black musicians of the time and always aimed to blend technique with soul.
611.q: Yeah, I liked, at that time I enjoyed the Elk [?], very much those bands for their musical ability. But I tell you, I was still advanced, you know, I was still thinkin' advanced. Now of all those bands that I heard, the band, white band that knocked me out the most was Jean Goldkette's Band. And as…

149.t: Would a white bandleader have gotten further?
149.s: He says doors, hotels and films would have opened sooner, but things are better now.
149.q: Well, during that time, of course, we didn't have the chance the white band leaders did. I couldn't have maybe been a little farther ahead. You know? I could, a few more doors could have been opened for me, quicker. I should say it that way. But, cause

428.t: Condon's mixed bands and the Dixieland closed shop
428.s: A discussion of integration in Dixieland bands and Condon's limited mixing.
428.ch: Wax Records, Broadway shows and Eddie Condon
428.q: Well, that -- that came in later years. Yeah. But it was restricted to those few that you named, you know, John Doe couldn't come in.

237.t: Differences between Black and white bands and who listened to whom
237.s: Goodwin says white and Black bands sounded distinct, white musicians came to hear Black bands, and jazz grew from the blues.
237.q: There was a difference. I can remember back in the '30s, early '30s and late '30s, that you would listen to a white band and you could tell this was a white band. You listened to a black band, you could tell this was a black band. There was a distinct difference; now however, the black bands tend…

75.t: Color consciousness and teasing about Blackness
75.s: Dance and Ramirez discuss prejudice against Rex for being big and dark, and the era's jokes about color versus later talk of Black pride.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: Well, to me it appeared just the other way around. I thought he was the classiest thing... You know, when Black Is Beautiful hit... He was...

103.t: What segregation cost jazz between 1926 and 1936
103.s: Jones says musicians were kept from playing with whom they wished, and the music lost much because of social conditions.
103.q: that we recapitulated. He didn't realize, as I said, it wasn't fashionable. But it's very difficult, Milt, can you imagine if we were all allowed the privilege with the social conditions being what they were - if we were all allowed the privilege 45 musicians to play with who we want to play with…

112.t: Business contact with whites, never at home
112.s: Wooding says he met whites like Lyons only in restaurants and clubs, never homes, and refused invitations that expected him to perform.
112.ch: South America and back in New York
112.q: Why do you say I stayed in Europe so long? Because today, you can meet him at the Park Sheraton or same hotel, something like that, but you'll never get to his home.
